Chapter III

The Language of Hopf Algebras

In this chapter we introduce the fundamental concepts of coalgebras, bialgebras, Hopf algebras and comodules which we shall use extensively in the sequel. We shall also prove that the algebras $GL(2)$ and $SL(2)$ of Chapter I are Hopf algebras.

## III.1 Coalgebras

The concept of a coalgebra is dual to the concept of an algebra in the following sense. Paraphrasing the definition of an algebra in I.1, we can say that an algebra is given by a triple $( A,\mu ,\eta)$ where A is a vector space and $\mu:A\otimes A\to A$ and $\eta:k\to A$ are linear maps satisfying the following axioms (Ass) and (Un).

(Ass): The square

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} A \otimes A \otimes A & \xrightarrow {\mu \otimes \mathrm {i d}} & A \otimes A \\ \downarrow \mathrm {i d} \otimes \mu & & \downarrow^ {\mu} \\ A \otimes A & \xrightarrow {\mu} & A \end{array}
$$

(1.1)

commutes.

(Un): The diagram

$$
k \otimes A \xrightarrow [ \searrow \cong ]{\eta \otimes \mathrm {i d}} A \otimes A \xrightarrow [ \downarrow ]{\mathrm {i d} \otimes \eta} A \otimes k
$$

(1.2)

commutes.

The axiom (Ass) expresses the requirement that the multiplication $\mu$ is associative whereas Axiom (Un) means that the element $\eta(1)$ of A is a left and a right unit for $\mu.$ The algebra A is commutative if, in addition, it satisfies the axiom

(Comm): The triangle

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} A \otimes A & \xrightarrow {\tau_ {A , A}} & A \otimes A \\ \searrow^ {\mu} & & \swarrow^ {\mu} \\ A & & \end{array}
$$

(1.3)

commutes, where $\tau_{A,A}$ is the flip switching the factors: $\tau_{A,A}(a\otimes a^{\prime})=a^{\prime}\otimes a.$

A morphism of algebras $f:(A,\mu ,\eta)\rightarrow(A^{\prime},\mu^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})$ is a linear map f from A to $A^{\prime}$ such that

(1.4)

$$
\mu^ {\prime} \circ (f \otimes f) = f \circ \mu \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad f \circ \eta = \eta^ {\prime}.
$$

We now get the definition of a coalgebra by systematically reversing all arrows in the previous diagrams.

Definition III.1.1. (a) A coalgebra is a triple $(C, \Delta ,\varepsilon)$ where C is a vector space and $\Delta :C\rightarrow C\otimes C$ and $\varepsilon:C\rightarrow k$ are linear maps satisfying the following axioms (Coass) and (Coun).

(Coass): The square

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} C & \xrightarrow {\Delta} & C \otimes C \\ \downarrow_ {\Delta} & & \downarrow_ {\mathrm {i d} \otimes \Delta} \\ C \otimes C & \xrightarrow {\Delta \otimes \mathrm {i d}} & C \otimes C \otimes C \end{array}
$$

(1.5)

commutes.

(Coun): The diagram

(1.5)

commutes.

(Coun): The diagram

$$
k \otimes C \xrightleftharpoons [ \varepsilon \otimes \mathrm {i d} ]{C \otimes C} \xrightarrow [ \mathrm {i d} \otimes \varepsilon ]{C \otimes k}
$$

(1.6)

commutes. The map $\Delta$ is called the coproduct or the comultiplication while $\varepsilon$ is called the counit of the coalgebra. The squares (1.5-1.6) express that the coproduct $\Delta$ is coassociative and counital.

If, furthermore, the triangle (Cocomm)

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} & C \\ \swarrow \Delta \\ C \otimes C & \xrightarrow {\tau_ {C , C}} & C \otimes C \end{array}
$$

(1.7)

commutes, where $\tau_{C,C}$ is the flip, we say that the coalgebra C is cocommutative.

(b) Consider two coalgebras $(C, \Delta ,\varepsilon)$ and $( C^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime},\varepsilon^{\prime})$ . A linear map f from C to $C^{\prime}$ is a morphism of coalgebras or a coalgebra morphism if

$$
(f \otimes f) \circ \Delta = \Delta^ {\prime} \circ f \quad a n d \quad \varepsilon = \varepsilon^ {\prime} \circ f.
$$

(1.8)

It is easily checked that the composition of two morphisms of coalgebras is again a morphism of coalgebras.

Let us give a few examples of coalgebras.

Example 1. (The ground coalgebra) The field k has a natural coalgebra structure with $\Delta(1)=1\otimes 1$ and $\varepsilon(1)=1.$ Moreover, for any coalgebra $(C,\Delta ,\varepsilon)$ , the map $\varepsilon: C\rightarrow k$ is a morphism of coalgebras.

Example 2. (Opposite coalgebra) For any coalgebra $C = (C, \Delta ,\varepsilon)$ set

$$
\Delta^ {\mathrm {o p}} = \tau_ {C, C} \circ \Delta .
$$

(1.9)

Then $( C, \Delta^{\mathrm{op}},\varepsilon)$ is a coalgebra which we call the opposite coalgebra and denote by $C^{\mathrm{cop}}.$

## III.2 Bialgebras

Let H be a vector space equipped simultaneously with an algebra structure $(H,\mu ,\eta)$ and a coalgebra structure $(H,\Delta ,\varepsilon).$ Let us discuss two compatibility conditions between these two structures.
